The [NASA Technical Reports Server][ref_ntrs] holds the engine record and the [Armstrong Flight Research Center][ref_nasa_armstrong] the institutional succession.

**The survey rests on 7,298 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,268 are report primaries by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary, being 17.4 percent. Of those primaries, 847 are Technical Reports Server records and 421 are Defense Technical Information Center reports. The survey includes the 208 research records cited in the argument above, each placed in the cluster its title describes, and 107 of those are report primaries. The median publication year of the dated records is 2007, and of those records 432, or 6.1 percent, appeared in or before 1960, the last year the X-7 flew, 2,845, or 39.9 percent, appeared before 2000, and 2,723, or 38.2 percent, appeared in 2015 or later.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when it is a NASA Technical Reports Server url or carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The same report can be reachable through Crossref and through the Defense Technical Information Center under two different labels**, and a rule keyed on where a record was found rather than on what it is would count such a report as secondary.

**The rule reaches the engine's documents and not the vehicle's.** The inlet, combustor and free-flight reports of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics are report primaries by this rule, and no record of the X-7 programme itself is among them. Journal papers by the engineers who did the work are not primaries by this rule either, so 17.4 percent is a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Eight subjects that this article's derivations and conclusions depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with every hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the X-7 and its Kingfisher derivative | x 7, lockheed x 7, kingfisher, aqm 60, ptv a 1, mx 883 | 0 |
| the Bomarc engine and the RJ43 | bomarc, rj43 | 1 |
| the Damköhler number and combustor residence time | damkohler, residence time, chemical time | 1 |
| the upper Mach limit of the airbreathing engine | maximum flight mach, upper bounds on the flight speed, mach limit, upper mach | 2 |
| the structural factor of safety | factor of safety, safety factor, safety factors | 0 |
| the learning curve in aircraft production | learning curve, experience curve, progress ratio, cost improvement curve | 3 |
| Fisher information | fisher information | 0 |
| the sampling theorem and channel capacity | sampling theorem, channel capacity, nyquist | 0 |

**The vehicle itself is the thinnest subject.** No research record carries the X-7, the Kingfisher, the AQM-60 or the programme's designators in its title, which is the institutional gap the paragraphs above describe. **Its engine lineage is barely better.** One record names the Bomarc engine or the RJ43, and it reports a long-term storage test of the production engine rather than its development. The free-jet and fuel reports cited above for the engine concern the XRJ47, a different ramjet of the same period.

**The two constructs that bound the engine are treated inside other subjects.** One record names the residence time or the Damköhler number, against the 180 flame-holding and blowoff titles in which the same competition between flow time and chemical time is studied as a stability limit. Two records name an upper Mach limit or flight-speed bound, and both concern the hydrocarbon-fuelled scramjet, so the ceiling of the subsonic-combustion ramjet that the article derives is reached in the literature inside performance analyses such as the one by Evans cited above rather than under its own name.

**The expendable method's arithmetic is thin in the cited literature as well.** No record names a factor of safety, so the values of 1.5 and 1.25 the article uses are representative figures, as the Epistemic State section records. Three records name the learning curve, and the founding paper by Wright states it as the cost of airplanes rather than under that name. No record names Fisher information, against the 109 titles that name experimental design, and no names the sampling theorem or channel capacity, because the papers by Nyquist and Shannon that the telemetry relation rests on are titled in the vocabulary of telegraphy and communication.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is the ramjet test vehicle, its inlet, its combustion, its heating, its boost and recovery, its instrumentation, the expendable method it stood for, and the engines and vehicles that inherited the problem. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. An inlet is also a tidal inlet, a culvert or the intake port of a piston engine. A flame holder also stabilizes the micro-combustors of portable power generation and industrial burners. A water ramjet is an underwater propulsor, and a ramjet and a specific impulse also belong to electric space thrusters and to the interstellar ramjet. A parachute is also a means of seed dispersal, a cause of parachutists' injuries and a corporate term. Telemetry also names the housekeeping data of satellites and the monitoring of software, and optimal sensor placement also serves water, traffic and power networks and the monitoring of buildings. A supersonic jet is also a molecular beam and a source of jet noise, and stainless steel at elevated temperature is also a subject of fire engineering and nuclear plant. Removal notices, records whose titles are a single unqualified word, biographical notes and obituaries are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or not works at all. A review of a book, a glossary, dictionary or reference entry, a news or other notice, and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and stay.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Optimal experimental design and the uncertainty of extrapolation outside aeronautics, bluff-body flame studies in laboratory and gas-turbine burners, combustion instability in liquid and solid rockets, supersonic parachutes for planetary entry, the trajectories of hypersonic glide vehicles, and studies of reusable launch vehicles each share a construct, a method or a contrast with this article's argument, so each is kept and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title in the survey has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

Established historical fact includes the start of development in December 1946, the MX-883 and L-171 designators, the PTV-A-1 designation and its change to X-7 in 1951, the failure of the first launch, the 130 flights between April 1951 and July 1960, air launch from B-29 and B-50 carriers, solid rocket boost followed by ramjet sustain, multi-stage parachute recovery with a nose spike, the stainless steel and nickel alloy construction, the X-7A-1 and X-7A-3 configurations and their dimensions and masses, the maximum Mach number of 4.31 and ceiling near 32 kilometres, the derivation of the AQM-60 Kingfisher, and the lineage of the engine into the Bomarc and the D-21.

Established engineering analysis includes every relation in the sizing sections. The isentropic stagnation relations, the normal shock total pressure ratio, the oblique shock normal Mach component, the recovery factor relation, the ideal ramjet specific thrust, the rocket impulse relation, the prediction variance of a fitted model, and the sampling theorem are standard results.

**Derived here and not taken from a source** are the fineness ratio of 19.6, the ram pressure ratios of 7.8 at Mach 2 and 152 at Mach 4, the Brayton efficiencies of 0.44 and 0.79, the normal shock recovery of 0.107 at Mach 4.31, the release Mach number of 0.45, the booster impulse of $1.87 \times 10^{6}$ newton seconds and the resulting velocity increment of 575 metres per second and burnout Mach number of 2.37, the boost acceleration of 13.2 g rising to about 16, the stagnation temperature of 1078 kelvin and recovery temperature of 985, the available combustion temperature rise of 922 kelvin, the specific thrust values, the residence time of 8.3 milliseconds, the parachute landing deceleration of 6.5 g, and the extrapolation variance figures. These follow by arithmetic from published dimensions and standard relations and can be reproduced or refuted by any reader with them.

Inference includes the central claim that the X-7's distinctive capability is epistemic rather than performance-related, namely that an expendable vehicle can interpolate across a limit where a crewed one must extrapolate toward it. That is the author's framing. The programme did not describe itself in those terms and no source consulted does.

Weakly supported are the representative values. The drop speed of 134 metres per second, the average boost mass of 3250 kilograms, the combustor temperature limit of 2000 kelvin, the combustor length and velocity behind the residence time, the descent speed of 8 metres per second, the spike penetration depth of half a metre, and the factor of safety values are all plausible figures for the class and not values taken from the design. The booster propellant mass is not stated in the sources consulted and the velocity increment therefore carries a corresponding uncertainty, though the conclusion that the booster delivers ramjet-starting Mach number is robust across the plausible range.

**The programme record is not public in the way the engine record is.** The X-7 was an Air Force and Lockheed programme under MX-883, and its own reports are not in the NASA archive that supplies the inlet, combustor, and free-flight sources cited throughout. The physics in this article therefore rests on excellent primary documentation and the programme narrative on secondary accounts, and the two should not be given equal weight.

Contested or unresolved in the sources consulted is the claim that the Kingfisher derivative outperformed the surface-to-air missiles fired at it and that the resulting embarrassment contributed to cancellation. It is widely repeated and no primary source establishing either the intercept statistics or the causal link was located. The exact top speed is given as Mach 4.31 in most accounts, and the earlier design speed near 1000 miles per hour is quoted alongside it without a clear statement of which configuration reached which.

A note on temporal position. This article carries an editorial date of 2025-10-13 and is written from current knowledge, including contemporary literature published well after that date.

## Conclusion

The Lockheed X-7 flew 130 times, reached Mach 4.31, and was never intended to survive its own programme.

Its engine explains its operating concept completely. A ramjet's compression ratio is one at rest, 7.8 at Mach 2, and 152 at Mach 4, so the engine is worthless standing still and unmatched at speed. The vehicle must therefore be thrown, and the booster that throws it delivers 1.87 million newton seconds, a velocity increment near 575 metres per second, and a burnout Mach number of 2.37, which is precisely where the engine becomes worth having. It does so at 13 g rising to 16, which is the first place where having no pilot is not a convenience but a requirement.

The spike is the second. A single normal shock at Mach 4.31 keeps a tenth of the total pressure, throwing away nine tenths of what the flight condition supplied, and a properly staged conical shock system keeps roughly forty percent. **That factor of nearly four is the difference between an engine and a duct**, and it is why the most conspicuous feature of the aircraft is a piece of pointed metal doing nothing visible.

Heat chooses the material without consultation. At Mach 4.31 the skin sits at 985 kelvin, or 712 degrees, which excludes aluminium and specifies steel. The same temperature rise that heats the structure also arrives at the combustor, leaving 922 kelvin of useful heat addition where a Mach 2 engine has 1600, and that shrinking allowance is the ceiling on the subsonic-combustion ramjet rather than any deficiency of the inlet.

What the vehicle demonstrated beyond its engines is harder to name and more durable. A crewed programme approaches a destructive limit and stops, so its estimate of that limit is an extrapolation whose variance grows as the square of the margin it keeps. An expendable programme crosses the limit and interpolates. **The X-7 could be flown to destruction and a crewed aircraft cannot, and that is a difference in what is knowable rather than in what is achievable.** The vehicle was not built for that reason and nobody in the programme described it that way, but it is the reason the architecture it pioneered, of air launch, rocket boost, airbreathing sustain, and telemetered destruction, has outlived every aircraft in this series so far.

The next article takes the [Aerojet X-8][ref_list_of_x_planes], the Aerobee sounding rocket, and asks what a designation means when the vehicle is not an aircraft at all.
